utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Carolyn Edgerton for the Prosecution, assisted by my colleague, Mr. Barney Thomas, and our case manager, Ms. Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, who are assisting us, along with our interns. My name is Gregor Guy-Smith, and, of course, Mr. Novak Lukic for Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Before we call the witness, one housekeeping matter. There's the swearing in of the new Judge this afternoon so this session will end at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you're bound by the declaration that you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To bring us back in focus, we were discussing Oslobodjenje right before we broke last time, and specifically we were having a discussion with regard to the issue of bias and objectivity, and I think time became a, I would say, not particularly our friend in terms of the discussion, so I'd like to pick up where we left off yesterday, if I may.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that you had -- you were at the point that we stopped yesterday explaining that in your view, and once again, correct me if I'm wrong, in your view, it wasn't necessary for a newspaper of record to be totally objective. I may be taking it a bit far for the moment, but I believe that was the gist of what you were maintaining yesterday right before we broke.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gist of what I was saying was that the newspaper -- the function of being a newspaper of record is only part of the reportorial side, news-gathering side, of any newspaper's function. It has an editorial and, let's say, opinion side as well. So I would certainly reject the notion that the newspaper as a whole is objective or impartial, even though it may function very effectively as a newspaper of record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that in mind, if I understand the distinction you're drawing, you're drawing a distinction between, as you've put it, the editorial side and the news-gathering function side.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am drawing that distinction and drawing a further distinction within the news-gathering side between its role as a newspaper of record and other reporting and news-gathering that it may do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So to the extent that you have a newspaper, for example, the one that's in issue, Oslobodjenje, and there are determinations made in the news-gathering side as to what news to gather and what news to report, in your view, does that affect the credibility or accuracy of the information which is being set forth in the newspaper? Or do you see -- do you see what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me put it in other terms, then. If the newspaper has a policy of only reporting one side of an issue, and by "reporting" I mean from the news-gathering function side, in not reporting both sides of the issue, do you believe that would affect whether or not it is in your terms a newspaper of record? Or do you believe a newspaper of record only dealing with something apart from that particular issue?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I view it as apart from. It could affect what it defines as worthy of being in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to Oslobodjenje, is it your opinion as a historian, that Oslobodjenje, in its news-gathering function during the period of 1991, 1992, and 1993, was a paper that was balanced in its news-gathering function?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it depends on when you look at it. It made a very conscious, calculated editorial policy change in I guess late 19 -- somewhere in the course of the second half of 1990 from being oriented to Yugoslav questions and reporting to being -- shifting more toward Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So that takes care of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just make sure I'm following you. Doctor, the question was related to the news-gathering function. You said it had a change in its editorial policy. My question to you is: Did the editorial policy also affect the news-gathering function policy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In what direction? In the same direction? In the same direction as the editorial policy went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is, the news-gathering, instead of focusing on -- instead of being a Yugoslav newspaper --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It became --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- it became a Bosnia-Herzegovina paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Much more parochial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But did that affect the policy of news-gathering to the extent that it was now limited to Bosnia-Herzegovina, was it still maintaining the same news-gathering policy as it did before, or did its news-gathering function have a change? In other words, as I understand the question, it looks like bias is being suggested here. Did you find that it -- to have a slanted reporting effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In fact, it continued to run a great deal of news about Yugoslavia principally from sources like TANJUG and other newspapers in the former Yugoslavia. But it relegated them further back in the number, in the issue. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without changing the content.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps reducing the length of the stories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whereas it had earlier had taken on the responsibility of reporting directly from Belgrade on activities of the federal presidency and parliament, it now relied upon sources other than its own reporters for that news. It was a shift of emphasis but not in terms of the basic approach to news-gathering in an effort to be balanced and to represent all sides and to cover all sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that's -- I think, your last answer to the Judge's question focuses - and I thank Your Honour - focuses specifically on the discussion that I'd like to have with you for a moment. You've just told us there "was a shift of emphasis but not in terms of the basic approach to news-gathering in an effort to be balanced and to represent all sides and to cover all sides. " With that answer in mind, as I understand that answer, that would mean during the period 1992 and 1993 for sure, 1991 I would also assume, that this paper was covering news as it related to Serbs who were being, for example, abused, mistreated or maltreated by the Bosnian army or others.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly speak into the microphone and speak up, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, counsel? Could you please speak into the microphone and speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have my question in mind?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know what you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me put it to you in an entirely different way, then. Are you familiar with the writings of I believe one of your colleagues, a gentleman by the name of David Rieff.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He wrote a book, I believe, called "Slaughterhouse and the Failure of the West."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a book you're familiar with, are you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, as a matter of fact, in that book Mr. Rieff discusses, among other things, that there was a discussion between the Deputy Chief Editor of the Sarajevo newspaper Oslobodjenje when the war started -- I'm sorry, the Chief Editor, who spoke with President Izetbegovic concerning the position that the paper was going to take with regard to the government, Izetbegovic's government, and that the paper was going to support that government; correct? That's something that Mr. Rieff discusses in his book.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that Mr. Rieff alleges took place in his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say he alleges it, do you recall as you sit here today where he received his source of information? Was that a primary source, meaning that he spoke to a person? Was it a secondary source, meaning that he got it from a piece of paper that was unrelated? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to tell you, as he relates it, that this would have come from a primary source, meaning a personal conversation that he had, would you contest that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You wouldn't accept it.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't have the information to verify that assertion of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And is the reason that you call it an assertion because you have some doubt about the information-gathering process that Mr. Rieff went through, or is it rather because you disapprove of the information that he related with regard to Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm simply saying it's been some years since I read that book. I don't recall the circumstances in which he frames the account of this conversation and therefore can't attest to the correctness of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. At line 11 of page --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me for two seconds, Your Honour. I'm having technical difficulties in terms of hearing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll speak up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, at line 11 of page 7, you say: "And when you say he alleges it, do you recall as you sit here today where he received his source of information? Was that a primary source, meaning that he spoke to a person? Was it a secondary source, meaning that he got it from a piece of paper that was unrelated?" I've got two questions. What information are we talking about, number 1? Is it the information that he spoke to Izetbegovic, saying that he's going to support the government, or is it some other information? And I ask that because if he spoke to Izetbegovic, then there's no question of what was the source of his information. He was part of -- he's part of the source. He was the person who negotiated with Izetbegovic. And what do we mean by "a secondary source," that is, a piece of paper? I'm asking that because if I'm the author of a document, then that paper is the primary source.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm absolutely with you, Your Honour, and I believe that as I -- as I look at the question as framed, the second part of it certainly needed more development, and I will deal with them both as you've requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Taking His Honour's question in mind, with regard to the first issue, that being of a primary source - once again going back to what David Rieff, as you've put it, asserts, that's his assertion - my question to you dealing with the issue of being a primary source is that David Rieff spoke to the Deputy Chief Editor concerning a conversation that was had between members of his department, specifically the Chief Editor, and Izetbegovic. So he personally did not speak to Izetbegovic but received the information from his Chief Editor. So when I'm talking about being a primary source, what I'm talking about is receiving information from in that situation, the participant in the conversation, assuming for purposes -- because you seem to have a question about it, assuming for purposes that it's true, that, in fact, that conversation occurred.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're fourth-hand, here, from Izetbegovic to some unknown person on the staff of Oslobodjenje to another person on the staff of Oslobodjenje to David Rieff to you to me. I can't assess the validity of that statement based on what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any -- do you have any reason to disbelieve it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any contrapositive reason to disbelieve it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say you don't have a contrapositive reason --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an outstanding fact that I believe contradicts it, but I'm skeptical.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that because of the way that you're hard-wired?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's I'd say a part of my general experience with these secondary accounts of what went on in that period and the difficulty of verifying a lot of these -- a lot of such conversations that are reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And yesterday, because of what you just said, yesterday we discussed the fact that when dealing with memoirs or diaries, some question with regard to whether or not those are issues that can be verified; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But it would be fair to say that you don't have the same kind of scepticism that you have with regard to that information that you have to the information that I've supplied to you with regard to Mr. Rieff's position, that Oslobodjenje had taken a position where they were going to support Izetbegovic's government; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my scepticism arises with a number of hands through which through which the information passes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of a gentleman whose name is Dusan Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And how do you know him? What do you know about him, before we go any further?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he has given some interviews and done some writing on the nature of the press in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Is he a member of -- is he a corresponding member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Academy of Sciences, the same group to which you have recently been made a member?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I told you that he was, would you have any reason to disbelieve that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of his -- as you said, you know that he did some writings with regard to the press. Are you aware of those writings? Did you have an occasion to take a look at any of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have some years ago but not recently. I can't really recall the nature of what he reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall that in 199 -- when you say you can't recall exactly what he reporter, let's see if this helps refresh your recollection as to what he reported and what you might have read. Do you recall that he discussed that in 1992 with regard to the issue of prisons or concentration camps, that of the stories that dealt with them numbering some -- somewhere around 98 or so, that most of them dealt with Serb prisons, and few or none dealt at all with what the Muslims were doing in that regard, from reporting of Oslobodjenje?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question is do I recall it? No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall that in 1993, out of approximately, give or take a few, 113 articles published by Oslobodjenje, all of which were talking about jails and concentration camps, not a single one was telling a story about jails, detainees, in which Muslims were holding Serbs or Croats. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would such information be of moment to you with regard to your reliance on Oslobodjenje as a source of accurate information when taking into account the answer you gave us moments ago concerning the balanced approach of this newspaper in its fact-finding or fact presentation function?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of a gentleman whose name is Vlado Mrkic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever come across -- and once again, let's see if this helps. You said, No, but I want to try and see whether or not this jogs your memory. He was a senior reporter at one point for Oslobodjenje. Does that help you at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll take that no further. Were you to re-examine the extent to which Oslobodjenje took, for example, a one-sided approach, and by that I mean a approach in which not only did they support the government, and by that I'm talking about the Bosnian Presidency, the Izetbegovic government, by editorial but also with regard to the facts that were adduced through the newspaper, would that shift your thinking with regard to your reliance on such a newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I actually would object to this question because I think it's been asked and answered. Dr. Donia has already stated that he does not accept that Oslobodjenje takes a one-sided -- or has taken a one-sided approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. Dr. Donia is being offered as a -- as an expert, and if you wish, I'm asking the -- I can ask the question independent of the matter whether he accepts or rejects my proposition as a hypothetical, that if the information were to be true, let me put it that way -- I'll reframe the question. Why don't I do that? And I'll make life easier for everyone. Because I was phrasing that question in a hypothetical fashion. Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I answer the question, Your Honour? I would be happy to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your counsel is objecting, and counsel on the opposite side is offering to rephrase. So for purposes of that particular question stands, the objection is upheld. Will you rephrase?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for your offer, but no, you may not, obviously. I'm asking the question as a hypothetical now, okay? If you were to take on board the information that Oslobodjenje took a one-sided approach in which they supported the government, not only in an editorial fashion but also with regard to their fact-finding and producing function, would that shift your thinking with regard to your reliance on this newspaper?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that hypothetical. I can answer a real-life question about --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- doctor --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap. That's the request from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking you the hypothetical question first, and if your answer is you can't answer the question, then I'm satisfied with your answer, and you've answered the specific inquiry given. We spent a fair amount of time discussing the -- and help me here, the "sest strategijskih ciljeva," or the six strategic objectives. Did I pronounce that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I didn't do so good this time. My team has been trying to teach me how to say that. I apologise. And I want to spend some time with you here in terms of some dates, okay? Because as I understand it, and specifically now dealing with the second strategic objective which I believe is the strategic objective in which you discussed that it transected an ethnic area on the map that you were shown. Are you with me? Or shall I pull up the map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I just want to know if you're with me in terms of the map you were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have map number 6 up on the board, please. It's P187. Wonderful. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were asked, I believe, whether or not the corridor, which is identified in the map as S.0. 2 would transect an ethnic area by Ms. Edgerton, and you replied that yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't ask him -- I'm sorry, Your Honour. I didn't ask him that question in respect of this map, just so we're all clear. I asked him that question in respect of the map which was -- bore the 65 ter number 9224.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But it deals with -- this map deals with the same area, does it not? Or would you need to see the other map first in order to make a determination as to whether or not we're speaking about the same area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that would only be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. That would be P338. As a matter of fact, can we have both maps up for the moment, because I want to focus -- I don't know if that can be done or not. Can we split the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll see if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right. I don't know if we can split the screen or not. I guess we -- we'll do it another way. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at P33 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you so much. Technology, wow, when it does work, it's quite impressive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at the map on the left-hand side of your screen, which is P338, and looking at the map on the right-hand side of your screen, which is P187, is the area where you drew the bar of your barbell roughly the area, or the area that is discussed on the corridor -- defined as corridor S.O. 2 on P187?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally. The map on the right shows the corridor much lower than it really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So it was actually higher than --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It hugged the Sava River, which is the boundary, in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So in P187, the representation is not particularly accurate, then, if you said it hugged the boundary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, great. Well, once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to say, do you know how wide it was at the corridor level, at its thinnest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At its thinnest, which was probably Brcko, as little as 2 or 3 kilometres. It widened very rapidly as it went west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was it at its widest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it widened into the entire Bosnian Krajina, perhaps, you know, 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you were to identify for us -- when you said Brcko, if you were to look at P187, I guess we're going to have to have that enlarged for a moment. I don't know if you can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you were to take a look at where the M and the B is in Semberija and go directly north, you will see -- I don't know if you can see it, there's some small lettering. Is that Brcko? Can you see it, or do you need it bigger?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is B-r-c-k-o, and it is right above the letter B with the name extending off to being above the letter M of Semberija. But right along the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be assistance to the Chamber if we had this marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. It can be marked, but we already have -- don't we already have this map? I thought you want to have it in with markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we don't -- we'd have to make a new exhibit of this map. I'm just -- in terms of correcting the corridor, I think it may be of some assistance to the Chamber just on this map to correct the actual corridor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I'm saying is on this map on the right, as it stands now, the correction has not been made yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So would you like to admit it like this as it is, without it being corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No. I was going to make some markings on it, if it was help to the Chamber, and then have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead and get the markings on, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If you could please ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think, first of all, if we could make the map bigger now, if that's possible to do. It might be easier to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could, starting at, I think you said Brcko, if you could then -- from Brcko, if you could go, as you've said, hugging the Sava River across the map as best you can. We understand that this is a ...

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could add that this changes over time during the course of 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The marking that you've just put there for right now, is that the 1992 -- is that the 1992 iteration?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changed at times daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, really.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It changed depending on the position of forces of the ABiH and the VRS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In terms of the -- who did you say?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, staying on this map just for a moment, if we could, if you could do me the kindest, if you look at where it says -- the word "corridor" is, if you go directly north from the -- between the D and the O of corridor, there's a village up there, is there not, which is the village of Sjekovac.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sjekovac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you circle --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if we could -- is red all right, or could we go into another colour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you draw a circle around Sjekovac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it on this map at this resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we make it bigger -- no, we can't, because the minute we do that -- I'm sorry. I have to have this -- I have to have this -- I found that by using two magnifying glasses. That's how I found it the other night at home. Could we have this marked for -- could we have this marked for identification as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is marked as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now could you please enlarge the map, because apparently once you've made a marking on it, you cannot change the map. So if you could now enlarge the map. I'm really interested in that one area right under the R of "Croatia." If there's a way of getting that part bigger, just so that the gentleman can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we're waiting just for the moment to see if we can get the map itself bigger, let me ask you some questions, which is that village is the village that was attacked in March of 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that village is a village that was attacked by the Croatian ZNG?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the people who lived in that village were --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when it was attacked in late March, that village was something that was of concern to a fair number of different people, and by that I mean that attack by the Croatians was condemned by Karadzic, I believe, among others, by members of the JNA and members of the BH Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, looking at that -- now we've lost it. That village bordering Croatia is an area where -- not only that village, but in that area there were a fair number of Serb inhabitants, were there not, it wasn't just that isolated village?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the expression noted by Mr. Karadzic in his May 12th speech concerning that particular corridor involved an area that had been attacked by the Croatians approximately, give or take, a month-plus. Put in other terms, about a month -- about a month and a couple weeks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect, when in his May 12th speech, and a 65 ter number would be wonderful. We make every effort to provide the same information to our colleagues when referencing a quotation, and this is a very lengthy Assembly session that I'm going to have to bend over backwards to try and find the relevant line of before the question is done, if we don't have some identification now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'll pull it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While I'm waiting to pull it up, what I'm driving at is this: Is that the second strategic objective as defined, which was putting -- placing a corridor in that area, covered a geographic place where Serbs had been attacked but a month before by the Croatians; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It included it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go ahead, are you abandoning the question to which you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I can abandon the question because I achieved the answer another way, but I'm going to come back to it once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not trying to make the record a mess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are because --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am. Well, let me abandon the question now because I got the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, so we don't mess up the record, for point of reference, it would be P188, the 16th session of the Assembly held on 12 May 1992, and it would be page 13 in which he states, meaning Karadzic: "The second strategic goal ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 13. What line?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 13, what line?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's not lines; it's paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the third starting with the words "The second strategic goal, it seems to me, is a corridor between Semberija and Krajina," which is -- that's the area we were just talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the village we were talking about that had been attacked, it would have been protected had that corridor been built?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply with respect to timing, it would have been protected at a later point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- had the military operations were not at that point -- at that time it could have been protected anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It could have been at that point, but the idea of having a corridor between the two points mentioned would have protected the village that had been attacked about a month before, right, if successful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that point on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During this time --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You can take the map off.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During this time, and we are now in May of 1992, there have been a number of developments with regard to questions asked to the international community and specifically to the Badinter Commission concerning various aspects of what I'm going to call for the moment the SFRY dissolution/secession issue; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was in November 1991 that Lord Carrington initially asked the first question, and now I'm summarising, which is was the situation such that Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, was in a state of dissolution or was there secession of the republics. Is that a fair --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific question which he asked of -- asked the Badinter Commission to resolve or to make recommendations on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll see if this refreshes your recollection with regard to the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have as a collective 1D001754, which is a collective exhibit of a number of the Badinter opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're calling it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm calling it up. If I could have page 1. And I apologise, this has not been translated into B/C/S, but I will read.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The first question was as follows, and I'm asking if this refreshes your recollection: "Serbia considers that those Republics which have declared or would declare themselves independent or sovereign have seceded or would secede from the SFRY which would otherwise continue to exist. Other Republics on the contrary consider that there is no question of secession, but the question is one of a disintegration or breaking-up of the SDRY as the result of the concurring will of a number of Republics." That was the general question. I'm asking for a legal opinion. That there were obviously two different views. One was secession and the other was dissolution. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The language is clear that it is a question of disintegration or breaking up versus secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fine. That question, depending on how it was to be answered, dramatically -- would dramatically affect the course of events, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you, as a historian, are aware of the fact that the distinction between a secession and disintegration was a hotly debated topic and one of major concern at that time, and by that I mean in late 1991.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That question was answered --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question was asked whether it was secession and disintegration, and the Badinter Commission made a determination that the former Yugoslavia, SFRY, was in the process of disintegration; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used the word "dissolution," if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The second opinion, if we could go to the next -- because I take it you don't recall the opinions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You don't recall the specific --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific language that they expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The second question and answer to that question dealt with something a little bit different, which is -- and was once again a question from Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we can have the next page of that exhibit, please, starting with the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to have the answer to these opinions to the first question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm more than happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going back to the first opinion, the Badinter Commission made a couple of determinations and ultimately in 2 -- I'm sorry, in 3, the opinion is as follows: "That the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is in the process of dissolution; that it is incumbent upon the Republics to settle such problems of state succession as may arise from this process in keeping with the principles and rules of international law, with particular regard for human rights and the rights of peoples and minorities; that it is up to those Republics that so wish, to work together to form a new association endowed with the democratic institutions of their choice." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, without discussing the specific legal ramifications of that opinion, have you had occasion, as a historian, to look at some of the murky aspects of it, since it creates a number of questions in and of itself with regard to how the various parties are going to respond?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This was not a necessarily bright-line approach, which is understandable, given the complexity of the situation that was presented. There was no clear way of the parties that were involved to make a determination precisely after the rendering of opinion number 1 as to how to proceed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. That's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the second question raised by Lord Carrington --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now if we could -- that starts at the bottom of the next page, which is here identified as page 183.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The second question was: "Does the Serbian population in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as one of the constituent peoples of Yugoslavia, have a right to self-determination?" Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And after considering a number of different matters, they came up with the following opinion, moving to the next page, and that is under 4. "(i) that the Serbian population in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia is entitled to all the rights concerned to minorities and ethnic groups under international law and under the provisions of the draft Convention of the Conference on Yugoslavia on 4 November 1991, to which the Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia have undertaken to give effect; and (ii) that the Republics must afford the members of those minorities --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: " -- and ethnic groups all the human rights and fundamental freedoms recognised in international law, including, where appropriate, the right to choose their nationality." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, we've discussed yesterday issues concerning minorities and ethnic groups in a general sense; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. We discussed the issue concerning national movements and how they were defined at some level; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And have you taken a look at this particular opinion, as a historian, to make a determination in your research with regard to what is the potential message or messages that are being given to the various people who were concerned, and specifically to those people who live in the area known as Bosnia-Herzegovina who are Serb?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And under this opinion, would it be fair to say that the guidance that they are receiving, among others, could be interpreted that they are in a position to advocate for the right to choose their nationality?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Going on to opinion number 3, the question asked there, once again by Lord Carrington, which is a relatively important question, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Counsel speak in the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again you are being requested to speak into the microphone, Counsel. The interpreters have difficulty hearing you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not that the others are not important, is: "Can the internal boundaries between Croatia and Serbia and between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia be regarded as frontiers in terms of public international law?" That was the question posed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this question is a question that begins to deal in a certain fashion with whether or not the former Republic of Yugoslavia can be broken up in terms of what would be considered to be a Westfalian view of state, and by that I mean that there are nation -- that it's a nation state with recognised geographic boundaries; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpret the question to be one of frontiers not of -- and referencing international law and not a question of Westfalian state or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of frontiers, what the effect of establishing new frontiers would be would be to redraw the geographic boundaries that existed within the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, would it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The committee, in regards to this question, because it found in its first opinion that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is in the process of breaking up, and that the Republics of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina "have sought international recognition as independent states ... mindful of the fact that its answer to the question before it will necessarily be given in the context of a fluid and changing situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We need to turn the page. Could we turn the page, please. I am continuing with the language on the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: " ... and must therefore be founded on the principles and rules of public international law. 2. The Committee therefore takes the view that once the process in the SFRY leads to the creation of one or more independent states, the issue of frontiers, in particular those of Republics referred to in the question before it, must be resolved in accordance with the following principles ..." and then those principles are listed. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, at this point in time, in late 1991, with regard to the question of the creation of one or more independent states, how many independent states had been created?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on what you mean by "created" and that would, I think, be a legal question that I couldn't address.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, how many -- how many states had applied for or had attempted to establish independence at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those are two different questions. At that time, if you're talking about prior to the 20th of December, no state had applied for independence, and at that point I would say Slovenia and Croatia had attempted to establish independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And had they been successful in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's, again, a legal question, I think. They had proclaimed independence, agreed to defer that proclamation of independence by 30 days or 90 days, proclaimed it again on 8 October, but were at that point unrecognised by the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did the European Community recognise Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was 15 January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe you're correct. And likewise, for Croatia, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what happened with regard to the question of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the -- given that we're paying close attention to the documents, it would be a good idea to actually go to the document and see what the decision of the Badinter Commission was in regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking you before we do that. Do you recall, and I appreciate your suggestion, sir, but do you recall what was the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was the status of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a full year. What date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, Dr. Donia, the latter part of 1991, after Lord Carrington has written his letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Status in what regard? There's been a number of questions here that broach on an area of expertise that's pretty much on the edge of Dr. Donia's area with some legal connotations, and I think we're getting back there again. I've let them go, but my question remains, status in what regard?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, were they recognised -- was Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as being independent?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's an unfair question. We don't know by who, we don't know in what way, and we don't know on what basis. So I would object on that grounds, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Was Bosnia-Herzegovina recognised as being independent by the European Community?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what date?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: December 1991.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During that period of time, December of 1991, are you aware of discussions that were being had between the United States Secretary-General and the representative of the European Community Mr. Genscher with regard to the recognition of these states? And by "these states" I mean specifically Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United States did not have a Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The United Nations. Excuse me. Thank you so much for the correction. The United Nations Secretary-General.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was concern at that time about the recognition of any -- and I'm talking, once again, in December of 1991 -- excuse me, let me expand that to November and December of 1991, that there was concern with regard to what the effect would be, and by that I mean peace or conflict, if there was recognition by the European Community of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton. There's an objection, sir. Your friend is on her legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I didn't see her, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Concern on whose part, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Concern on the part of the United Nations' Secretary-General?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Moving to the next opinion, if we could, and that's opinion number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In this opinion, the commission was asked to recognise the -- was asked by the Minister of Foreign affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to recognise that republic, correct, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm looking at the very first paragraph, "In a letter dated 20 December ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who would that have been, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Haris Silajdzic, but I can't see definitively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And was he -- in terms of the way that we've identified the groupings, was he a Muslim, a Serb, or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Bosnian Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The commission made a determination here, and I'm going to the next page if we could, and if we could go -- thank you. Go down. First of all, the commission made a number of notes, and I'm referring you now to note number -- under 2. It noted that the Socialist Republic for Bosnia-Herzegovina will become a member of the new Yugoslav community, and there are two conditions that are there; right? That's what -- that's what the Socialist Republic for Bosnia-Herzegovina had indicated they were prepared to do.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Reference is here for the platform that was approved on 15 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that platform includes a -- includes a community of Serbia and Croatia, right, at a minimum?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And is that a federation? Is that a co-federation? What would that community be defined as?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We looked at this document yesterday, and it doesn't specify. It only specified that the relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia and the relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia had to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But this says something -- this doesn't talk about a relationship here. This says the new community must include which is different than a relationship between. So how do you define it must include?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that will be my last question for this session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll stop now and pick it up when we come back. Would this be a convenient moment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be a very convenient moment. We'll take a break and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I realise Madam Edgerton is on her feet. Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Only to announce an addition to the appearances. Our colleague Ms. Sutherland has joined us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Welcome, Ms. Sutherland. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question was, with regard to the issue found at (ii) whether or not your discussion of relationship between the communities is the same as the word here "include." When you were talking yesterday about the relationship between the communities, were you envisioning that the new community should include these constituent parts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, fine. The conclusion of this opinion is, at paragraph number 4: "In these circumstances, the arbitration commission is of the opinion that the will of the people of the Bosnia-Herzegovina to constitute the SRBH as a sovereign --"

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To the top of the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "As a sovereign and independent State cannot be held to have been fully established." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that was the state of play as of 11 January 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard, and I'm going to do this rapidly, if you could take it on faith that opinions 5, 6, and 7 all deal with essentially the same question. Opinion number 5 being recognition of the Republic of Croatia, 6 being Macedonia, and 7 being Slovenia, and in each of those situations the commission found that those republics met the necessary conditions for recognition by member states of the European Community on the 11th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Moving to, then, opinions 8, 9, and 10, collectively, but starting with opinion, obviously, number 8 that is found on page 84 of this particular grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have page 84, please. I'm sorry, in e-court it's page 15 of 22. And if we could go to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now we are in the month of May 1992, specifically the 18th of May. Once again, the commission has received letters from -- a letter from Lord Carrington with regard to a number of particular questions. But before we address those questions, by that point in time there had been a decision to withdraw the JNA from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had there not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the questions asked by Lord Carrington, moving over to the next page now, which would be page 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll just move over a bit. I think it may be -- yes, perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The questions -- two of the questions that I asked is: In its opinion of number 1 of 29 November 1991, the Arbitration Commission was of the opinion "that the SFRY (was) in the process of this dissolution." Can this dissolution now be regarded as complete? 2. "If this is the case, on what basis and by what means should the problems of the suck succession of states arising between the different states emerging from the SFRY be settled"? Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Kind of a burning question at the time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the answer without -- I'm not going to go through all of the issues concerning various positions that were taken, but the answer ultimately, which is found on page 18 with regard to opinion number 8, is predicated, among other things, upon the commission's reliance of its opinion number 1, and I'm moving towards the bottom part of the page where it says, number 1, "In its opinion ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go down a little bit, please. Up. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at number 1. "In its opinion number 1 of 129 November, the Arbitration Commission found that: A state's existence or non-existence had to be established on the basis of universally acknowledged principles of international law concerning the constituent elements of a state." And then the next bullet point is: "The SFRY was at that time," referring to the 29th of November, "still a legal international entity, but there had been a desire for independence expressed by ..." and then it's mentioned who this was expressed by. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the wording, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the question of the existence or non-existence of a state, had that issue, and I'm not talking about it legally, I'm talking about the reaction of the various individuals or parties, been satisfactorily defined, do you think?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a compound question, Your Honour, and we do have a guideline on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's not a compound question, but I'm happy to rephrase it, if Ms. Edgerton is confused. It's absolutely not a compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm not going to get into it. I'll rephrase the question. It's not compound, but I'll rephrase if she has difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you may. But before you do, let me just say to Dr. Donia: Dr. Donia, the process that we follow is once I -- the opposite counsel stands up to object and I call her name, please -- could you please stop and not answer. The idea of her standing at that stage is to intervene before you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I feel since it was asserted that I was confused, I should explain that my confusion arises from the question being with respect to individuals or parties, and I would ask that it be broken down to two questions, individuals and parties, and that we be informed as to what "various" means. That's wherein my confusion might lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the existence or non-existence of a state, as a historian, do you believe that your research revealed whether or not Izetbegovic was clear about, in his mind, what the definition of "state" was -- in this context?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say whether he was clear or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you say whether or not Mr. Karadzic was clear?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearer, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, would it not be helpful to get the witness's opinion on those questions if you put to him what that position was, what their reaction was to that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then at least he can comment on that. Right now it looks like you're asking him to go into the minds of these people to find out what they thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you aware of what Mr. Izetbegovic's position was with regard to the findings of the Badinter Commission concerning opinion number 8?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, going one by one, he agreed with the first bullet. He agreed with the second bullet. I don't know what his view was on the third bullet. I don't know whether he'd agree with the fifth bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the third bullet, you're referring to the language starting with "The composition ..." just so the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the fourth bullet, you said nothing about that, and you went to the fifth bullet.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. One, two, three, four. Four is "Recourse to force in different parts of the Federation had demonstrated the Federation's impotence." I don't know what his conclusion or position was on that issue. I think he had a position that was consistent with point -- with the next-to-last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which starts with the words "The SFRY ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And certainly agreed with the last point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Karadzic, can you tell us what his reaction was and his position? Excuse me, let me make that simpler. Are you aware of what Mr. Karadzic's position was with regard to the findings of the Badinter Commission's concerning opinion number 8?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The ultimate opinion was that -- and that's found at the next page, section 4: "That the process of dissolution of the SFRY referred to in opinion number 1 of 29 November 1991 is now complete and that SFRY no longer exists." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you specify what date we're speaking of here?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to the date of "Paris, 4 July 1992."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that point 4? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "The arbitration commission is therefore of the opinion: That the process of dissolution of SFRY referred to in his opinion number 1 of 29 November 1991 is now complete and that the SFRY no longer exists."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the date is 4 July 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, of course, with that in mind, that the process of dissolution is now complete and SFRY no longer exists, there are, for our purposes of discussion, two remaining questions that I'd like to discuss with you, which are contained in opinions number 9 - excuse me - and opinion number 10. Once again, a letter which had been received from Lord Carrington in May of 1992, referring back to whether or not the dissolution of SFRY had been complete, the question is: "If this is the case, (is the dissolution of the SFRY now complete?)" --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go to the next -- no, it's right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "... on what basis and by what means should the problems of the succession of states arising between the different states emerging from the SFRY be settled"? That was the question posed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the question Lord Carrington posed in his letter of 18 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the commission responds to that question by listing out - and going to the next page, please - one specific issue initially, and I'm going right above number 4 -- no, I won't do that. I'm going to number 4: "The arbitration commission is therefore of the opinion ..." and then there are listing of bullet points as to what the opinion is with regard to the issue of successor state; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on the declaration adopted by the European Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that. But what happens here at number 4 is that an opinion is rendered, and these are the bullet points with regard to the opinion that the same commission that we've been discussing in the previous eight opinions is rendering concerning the issue proposed by Lord Carrington; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The arbitration commission --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Donia, I hate to interrupt you. If you could answer my question, I'd appreciate it. Then of course you can explain it. This -- if you could answer my question yes or no, so we're clear on the record that this is the opinion of this body that we've been talking about in the previous eight opinions concerning the questions posed by Lord Carrington; right? That's what it says: "The Arbitration Commission is therefore of the opinion ..."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And then it lists a number of bullet points as to what its opinion is; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And it concludes -- it concludes, after going through those bullet points, the last bullet point being: "Since, however, no specific question --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: "Since, however, no specific question has been put to it, the commission cannot at this stage venture an opinion on the difficulties that could arise from the very real problems associated with the succession to the former Yugoslavia." Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is dated, once again, the 4th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Finally, the last opinion that I wish to discuss with you briefly deals with the very specific issue of -- I'm sorry, yes, the very specific issue of a successor state and the question asked was: "In terms of international law, is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia," which we have normally been calling here FRY, "a new State calling for recognition by the Member States of the European Community in accordance with the joint statement on Yugoslavia and the Guidelines on the recognition of new states in Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union adopted by the Council of the European Communities on 16 December 1991." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Then the opinion is found on the last page of this particular series. That's at section 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There are two bullet points. I'm going to refer to the first bullet point there under 5: "Consequently, the opinion of the arbitration is that," the first bullet point, "the FRY (Serbia and Montenegro) is a new state which cannot be considered the sole successor to SFRY." Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And once again, the date of that is 4th July 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I move this collected exhibit of those opinions into evidence as defendant's next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They are so admitted. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it, in your estimation as a historian, be fair to say that questions concerning the relationships between the various, and by that I mean Croatia, FRY, and Bosnia-Herzegovina as independent states, as confederated states, was up to at least July 1992 in a dynamic situation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not confederated states. Unquestionably the relationship -- the relationships among those three was in a dynamic situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And specifically with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the situation was, for purposes of maintaining the same thinking process, clearly more dynamic than that of Croatia which had been recognised as a state and that of FRY which had been recognised --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- by -- it was not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not more dynamic than the relationship with the other two, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The issue with regard to the -- the issue with regard to FRY as a unit, and by "unit" I mean a state, had been resolved, and by that I mean FRY had been created, that it was not a successor state to SFRY so it did not necessarily obtain all of the duties and obligations that SFRY had obtained, but it was a compact unit. And I did put more in that than I should have, and I do apologise, Ms. Edgerton, so let me pull back. FRY was recognised by the commission as an independent state.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission had no authority to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I didn't ask that --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to recognise that as an independent state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would the speakers kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the authority of the commission. I asked you whether it was recognised.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking you to please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Croatia had been recognised as an independent state months before; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by some other states.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As had Slovenia.
